P1.evidence: P1a miss, with unusually direct evidence: nothing was read back and the prospect opened with 'I don't know what I'm doing here. I don't know what this is, actually.' The rep recovered well — 'These calls are very simple' — but the check is about making them feel seen from their own application, and there was no application in the room. P1b partial: three of four parts — 'I just want to understand what's going on, what have you tried, and where you're trying to get to in terms of fitness, health.' 'What you need' was not framed. He did add a clean takeaway — 'if there's alignment, we can talk about it, for sure. If not, that's fine, too' — which he then honoured at the end. P1c hit: 'Sounds good?' asked and agreed. P1d hit: 'walk me through, like, what's been going on? Like, what's the main thing you're trying to fix now?', preceded by a good source question, 'How did you actually found out about us?'

P2.evidence: The weakest baseline in the batch. P2a partial — height was asked ('And how tall are you?') and weight was volunteered and echoed; age was volunteered ('I'm 34 now') and never asked. P2b miss, and consequential: the rep never asked what he does for work, yet twice asserted 'you're a businessman, I'm a business guy too' and built the whole money conversation on that assumption. For a prospect who turned out to have zero liquid cash, establishing the actual occupation and income was the one baseline question that would have changed the call. P2c and P2d miss — no health conditions, no injuries, no movement limitations, on a 34-year-old who has never exercised in his life and is about to be sold ballistic loaded training. P2e miss — the current calisthenics routine and its frequency were volunteered ('Calisthenics is also like 30 minute workout and it's in my house'), never asked. P2f miss — three weeks in, and the rep never asked what results he was already getting, which would have been the natural setup for the free-alternative objection that later killed the deal. P2g hit and genuinely good — 'how about nutrition? How do you treat your body?', then 'do you follow any diets?', then careful clarification of the vegetarian boundaries including fish, eggs and dairy. P2h and P2i miss — sleep and energy never raised, though the rep later asserted energy benefits he had no baseline for.

P3.evidence: The strongest questioning in the call, and it still failed at the decisive check. P3a hit — 'what's the main thing you're trying to fix now?' P3b and P3c miss — the mobility/strength/energy menu was never offered and the 'something you want to do but can't' question was never asked. P3d hit, run twice and well: 'Sorry to cut you off, but like, why is that so important to you?' and when the answer was 'I don't know', he held the silence — 'Just think about it for a second. What's the reason that you actually want to get in shape? Why?' That produced the mirror answer and the health answer. P3e hit — 'in three months, or let's say six months down the road, when you actually see the changes in your body... what opens up to you?', and when Jorge said he did not understand the question, the rep rephrased rather than dropping it. P3f partial — the impact on others was asserted rather than asked: 'So you want to show up for them. So every single day when you wake up and you see their faces, you know what's your why behind that.' P3g hit — the rep drove to longevity and legacy properly, using the father contrast and then the sit-to-stand longevity test: 'if you want to be at 75 and be supple... this is a scientific measurement of your longevity.' P3h miss, and this is where the call was actually lost. The reflect-back never happened because the prospect refused to supply a deep why: 'It won't change my life. That's what I mean' and 'No, definitely not.' The rep pushed once — 'Do you really believe that if you change your body, how you feel with your body, how you show up, that won't change your life?' — got 'it's just gonna add something to my personal profile', and then capitulated: 'I like it. That's good enough.' It was not good enough. The prospect had just told him the outcome was worth about as much as learning French or taking up chess, and the rep proceeded to a $6,000 ask on that basis.

P4.evidence: The best-run root-cause phase in the batch by some distance. P4a hit — asked in the frame and pursued with 'Never?', producing a detailed three-attempt history. P4b partial — the outcomes were narrated rather than elicited; the rep never asked 'what happened with that' directly. P4c hit — 'have you thought about deep down what's been behind that, that you didn't enjoy or wanted to actually make that change in the past?' P4d hit, and the best single move on the call: when Jorge gave the standard excuse ('I have no time to exercise'), the rep declined to accept it — 'Well, it depends. We're all busy, yeah?' — and that pressure produced the truth: 'It's that I don't like it enough... I'd rather watch a TV series than work out.' That is the actual obstacle, surfaced properly. P4e partial — having got there, the rep did not let Jorge name the structural gap; he pivoted straight into a kettlebell feature pitch ('So the beauty about kettlebells is you can do it in home...'). The gap he needed named — no accountability, no programming — went unnamed until the prospect raised it himself during the price objection. P4f partial — the line exists in the script almost for this exact prospect, who is currently self-coaching from YouTube, and it was run reactively at 00:36:26 ('the difference is in the accountability, especially') rather than in Phase 4 where it would have built the case before the number.

P5.evidence: The consequence frame was never built, and the material for it was exceptional. The prospect handed over a fully formed two-year picture unprompted — a father who is 75, 'looks 95', never exercised and is now 'a crippled old guy', set against a father-in-law of the same age who trains and is 'amazing' — plus his own line, 'if I don't do it today, then tomorrow will be harder than yesterday.' P5a miss: 'if nothing changes, what does life look like' was never asked, and with that father sitting in the conversation it would have written itself. P5b and P5c miss: no settling question, no 'why not'. P5d partial: the rep used the exact scripted phrase — 'So this is the, like, the moment of drawing the line in the sand. And like, I'm doing something and not just talking about it' — but ran it at 00:38:54, after the price and after the prospect had already said he had no money, where it read as pressure rather than as a decision point. Phase 5 exists to make the price feel small before the price is named; here it arrived after, and did nothing.

P6.evidence: P6a hit and correctly sequenced before the number: 'If you had the right training, a simple nutrition, and someone like Trevor in your corner, all built around your life actually, would you agree that you would get to your goal?' Answer: 'definitely.' P6b partial — the go-all-in question was never asked before presenting; its nearest equivalent, 'Is there anything else holding you back?', ran at 00:34:31, after price, as objection isolation. And the answer it produced was contaminated: seconds earlier Jorge had said 'I don't know if specifically Trevor', which the rep treated as a yes and moved past, so the isolation was never clean. P6c miss, and it is the structural failure of the call. The script says move forward only on a clear yes and return to Phase 5 if hesitation surfaces. Hesitation had surfaced twice and been ignored: the prospect explicitly rejected the deep why ('It won't change my life'), and then flagged the price before it was named ('Sounds expensive. That's what I'm waiting to hear'). The rep proceeded through the delivery walkthrough and into the number both times, and never went back to Phase 5.

P11.evidence: The deal never reached the phase — the prospect refused the offer and the financing outright, so payment, onboarding, agreement and welcome-email steps were all unreachable. Worth recording as a sequencing note rather than a score, though: the rep attempted step 2 before step 1 and before the price existed. At 00:32:35 he said 'next thing is we need to book you with Trevor', and the prospect had to interrupt to stop him — 'Before that, I'd like to understand the full picture. It sounds expensive.' Booking the onboarding call before naming the number, and before any payment, inverts the phase.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete Objection C run in this batch, and still only half the play. Ran correctly: ISOLATE FIRST — 'finances aside, are you 100% sure that you can actually achieve your goals with Trevor?' and 'Is there anything else holding you back?'; the should-versus-how reframe in the rep's own idiom — 'We're business guys, we can work things out, yeah? So we don't have anything set in stone, like payment plans, but if there's a will, there's a way'; permission for the financial conversation, close to verbatim — 'So you're open for an open discussion about finances?'; and then three of the six financial-picture items — liquid cash ('what's your liquid cash right now on your hand?', answer zero), credit card usage, and credit score. He also pushed properly on the vague claim rather than accepting it: 'when you say you don't have money, what do you exactly mean by that? You don't have the full amount?' Not run: what is left over each month after bills, how many credit cards, available credit total per card, and used versus available — which are precisely the questions that determine whether a financing partner can do anything for a man with zero cash. Investments were also never asked. Two flaws beyond omission. First, the isolation was not clean: 'I don't know if specifically Trevor' was treated as a yes. Second, the rep offered financing on the back of a credit-score answer of 'Amazing. 10.', which is not a credit score on any scale and was not clarified.

Trigger present in substance and at length — the mountain-bike analogy is a textbook not-the-right-time: 'I would first go and buy a small, used bicycle... and then after a year, then I'll see if I'm prepared to spend 6k, but not now.' The rep ran the play in reverse. He agreed with it and then volunteered the objection on the prospect's behalf: 'Yeah, yeah, makes sense. Look, maybe it's not the time of the, not the right time in your life for these changes.' None of the six moves ran. The omission that matters most: 'the longer you wait the harder this gets' was the prospect's own thesis, delivered unprompted at 00:07:28 — 'I'm 34. I'm not 24 anymore. And if I don't do it right now, every day that passes from now on, it's harder, not easier, as it was before.' The rep had a written rebuttal in the prospect's own words, thirty-five minutes old, and did not reach for it. In fairness, the disqualification may well have been the correct commercial judgement given zero cash; the play still should have run before conceding.

Soft trigger and a credit to the rep: the prospect reached for the delay himself — 'I don't know what would be the next step. Like, for me to think about it and give you an answer? Or how does it go?' — and the rep refused to grant it, going straight to the isolation question instead. That is the right instinct and the right sequence. It scores partial rather than hit because none of the Objection A follow-through ran once the isolation was answered: no 'what makes you feel it can', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision', which had obvious purchase on a man with three abandoned attempts behind him.

SCRIPT GAP, and the extreme case of the one already logged. The known gap covers 'a cheaper alternative already worked for me' as seen with a $29/month coach. Here the alternative is free YouTube calisthenics, it is currently working — three weeks, the longest streak of the prospect's life — and he constructed the comparison himself, feature by feature, conceding every point of Primal's superiority before choosing free anyway: 'One of them also has somebody that's following you up... Super amazing. That sounds amazing. But one of them is free. That's, I think, more amazing than the rest.' The rep improvised the only sensible line, differentiating on accountability and programming rather than content, and it earns the partial. But he opened by conceding the content is free ('Everything, all the knowledge, everything, it's on YouTube. You can look it up'), which handed the prospect his own case — 'Yeah, that's exactly my point.' Objection C cannot touch this, because the blocker is not capacity to pay; it is a functioning zero-cost substitute. A play is needed, and it should be built around the failure history rather than the feature set: this prospect has quit at two weeks three times, and is currently at three weeks.

SECOND SCRIPT GAP — no low-cost entry rung. The prospect articulated the want precisely and reasonably: prove the interest cheaply, then commit capital. 'I would first go and buy a small, used bicycle... and then ride it a bit, and then see if I really like it, and then see if that's really a priority... and after a year, then I'll see if I'm prepared to spend 6k.' Nothing was offered between free content and $6,000 — no guide, no short trial, no single onboarding session, no deposit that holds a price. The rep went straight from $6,000 to third-party financing to goodbye. Whether the business wants a lower rung is a strategy decision, but the absence of one turned a motivated prospect into a clean loss with no residual relationship and nothing sent.

notes: Paradoxically one of the better-run calls in the batch and a correct outcome: the rep asked real why-questions, refused the 'I have no time' excuse and got to the truth ('I don't like it enough'), pre-empted a think-about-it, ran the most complete money play of the batch, and disqualified cleanly rather than discounting. Three things to coach. First, he ignored two clear stop signals — the prospect flatly rejecting the deep why ('It won't change my life') and pre-flagging the price ('Sounds expensive') — and pressed on to the number both times instead of returning to Phase 5, which the script tells him to do. Second, Phase 5 was never run at all, despite the prospect handing him the single best consequence image in the corpus: a 75-year-old father who looks 95 and cannot get up. Third, and most fixable, he conceded the not-the-right-time objection instead of quoting the prospect's own words back at him from thirty-five minutes earlier. Above the rep's head: this lead should never have reached a closer. He came from an Instagram ad he had not sought, did not know what the call was, had zero liquid cash, and measured fitness spending against a $25 tub of protein. That is a qualification failure upstream, and it cost forty-three minutes of closing time.
